_meta.title: AI Transparency Index
_meta.lede: How openly the major AI providers let the public see what their AI costs — in dollars, in data, and in water and energy. We grade transparency, not the underlying footprint: whether a real figure is findable at all, and who had to surface it. 'Not disclosed' is a finding, not a gap to paper over.

axes.label: Environmental impact
axes.note: Capacity-weighted water & energy disclosure across known AI data center sites. Scored below.

axes.label: Pricing
axes.note: Five dimensions of what a provider tells you about what you are buying, all read from primary sources. Scored below. Providers tell you the price and when it will change; none tells you what you get for it.

axes.label: Data practices
axes.note: Criteria not yet defined — Not yet scored. The only axis still unbuilt.

_meta.methodology: We grade three independent axes — pricing, data practices, and environmental impact — separately, and never average them into one score. Four-state system: 🟢 Transparent (the company discloses it itself) · 🟡 Partial (a real figure is public, but only via a regulator, utility, or watchdog — not the company) · 🔴 Opaque (nothing public) · ⚪ Not yet assessed (we haven't checked yet — which is not the same as opaque). For environmental impact specifically: we track each provider's known AI data center sites and grade every site on water/energy disclosure, then roll them up into a capacity-weighted average — bigger sites carry more weight. That means a large opaque site can't hide behind a small transparent one, and one bad site doesn't sink an otherwise-open provider either. Every grade links to its sources — 42 of 42 on the environmental matrix and 40 of 40 on the pricing one, every URL checked. The pricing axis was defined and scored on 2026-08-25 across five independent dimensions — API rate card, consumer allowance, consumer context window, price-change notice and model-retirement notice — graded separately and never averaged, on the same 4-state scale. Its provider set deliberately differs from the environmental one: it covers the eight companies selling AI directly to consumers or developers. Data-practices criteria aren't defined yet, so that axis is still marked 'Not yet scored.'

grade_legend.label: Partial — public only via regulator, utility or watchdog

caveats: Site coverage is currently 12 sites across 7 providers and expanding over time — that reflects our research pace, not a judgment on any provider we haven't listed yet. Early-stage campuses with no meaningful operating capacity yet (e.g. Meta's Hyperion, the Stargate expansion sites) are tracked but shown without a capacity weight until they're running. Pure-play colocation landlords (e.g. Equinix, NTT, CyrusOne) aren't scored here yet — they publish fleet-wide efficiency rather than per-AI-site figures, and need their own treatment.
Most 🟡 grades today exist only because of local advocacy groups and utility-records work — not because any law requires the company to disclose. That gap is itself part of the story.
Grades are re-verified periodically, not continuously — a site can move between checks.
This is Legerly's independent read of public information, not a regulatory finding. Tell us if we got something wrong.

detail.title: Disclosure quality by dimension
detail.note: A closer look at how complete each company's own environmental reporting is, across six disclosure dimensions. This lens grades a company's self-reporting rather than the 'can the public find out at all' question the site scores above answer — so here 🟢 means good disclosure, 🟡 partial, 🔴 none or poor. We grade what each company DISCLOSES about the AI compute it controls, not the footprint itself. Rented-vs-owned rule: each company is graded only on what IT publishes, regardless of who owns the building — so a renter that stays silent (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI) has disclosed nothing, while one that publishes facility detail gets credit. Cross-board: no company separates AI-specific from general data-center footprint, none discloses indirect (power-generation) water — LBNL estimates indirect ≈ 12× direct — and there is no U.S. federal water-disclosure mandate as of mid-2026.
caveats: We grade DISCLOSURE quality, not true environmental performance. A low grade means opacity, not necessarily high impact — a genuine closed-loop site (e.g. Abilene) may use little water yet still score 🔴 for not publishing numbers.

Withdrawal ≠ consumption, and direct ≠ indirect. No company discloses indirect (power-generation) water, which LBNL estimates at ~12× direct — so every 'water positive' claim understates the true system footprint.

Some gradings are genuinely ambiguous and are flagged, not silently resolved: Meta's site-level cell now sits between 🟡/🟢 — it reports electricity and emissions per facility but no per-site water, and we graded the missing metric rather than the present ones; Microsoft's ‘water positive’ claim is still aggressive, but for a narrower reason since Aug 2026 — it now publishes withdrawal per location while keeping consumption in aggregate.
Conflicting figures are shown as ranges, not picks — e.g. Google Council Bluffs 2024 ≈ 1.0B gal consumed / 1.3B potable / 1.4B withdrawn depending on source and metric.

The xAI/OpenAI/Anthropic non-disclosure finding was re-verified on 2026-08-25 against reporting from Aug 2026, not left resting on the Dec 2025 trackers — a verified absence expires too. The underlying fact, that no company environmental report exists, is directly checkable from the absence of any such document. California's SB 253 requires Scope 1 and 2 reporting from large companies operating in the state starting November 2026, so these rows may finally move within a year; classifying the bulk as Scope 3 would delay most of it to 2027.

pricing.title: Pricing transparency — by dimension
pricing.note: What a provider tells you about what you are buying. Same 4-state scale as the page above, applied to five independent dimensions and never averaged. THE HEADLINE FINDING: providers are good at telling you the price and when it will change, and almost uniformly silent on what you get for it. Six of eight commit to a quantified price-change notice and five of those land on exactly 30 days with a cancel-before-renewal right — this is the most standardised disclosure in the industry. Set against that, all eight publish no usage allowance at all. Of 27 consumer plans across 8 providers, 26 publish no usage allowance — and the one exception is a feature sub-limit, not a general allowance. Note the provider set differs from the environmental axis above: this table covers the eight companies that sell AI to consumers or developers directly, so Amazon and Meta are absent and Perplexity, Mistral, DeepSeek and Microsoft appear.

grade_legend.label: Published by the provider, and usable
Published but incomplete, unquantified, or late

caveats: This axis grades DISCLOSURE, not value for money. A plan can be excellent and still score 🔴 here for not saying what it includes, and a cheap plan gets no credit for being cheap.

Price-change and model-retirement notice have now been read directly on all eight providers' own terms and docs — no cell on this axis rests on a secondary source. The single remaining ⚪ is Microsoft's API rate card, which is not graded because Copilot is sold as a subscription with no per-token price to publish; that is a different business model, not a disclosure failure.
The allowance finding comes from Legerly's own plan-limits data, re-verified 2026-08-24, where every plan carries a provenance value and a source. It is a count, not an impression.

Price-change notice turned out BETTER than we expected when we started this axis, and it is recorded that way. Both OpenAI and Anthropic give consumers 30 days and make increases effective at next renewal so the subscription can be cancelled first. An axis that only found bad news would not be evidence.

rate_card.note: Per-token rates for every model published on its own developer pricing page; re-verified against that page on 2026-08-24, when gpt-5.6-sol had moved $5/$30 → $4/$20.

allowance.note: The only absolute consumer figure any provider publishes is OpenAI's, and it is a feature sub-limit rather than an allowance: Go users get 10 messages every 5 hours after enabling Thinking. Worse, between our 2026-07-28 and 2026-08-08 checks OpenAI DELETED the one general cap anyone published — '160 GPT-5.5 Instant messages per 3 hours' — replacing it with limits that 'can be dynamic and may vary'. ChatGPT Plus is now the most expensive consumer tier of any provider carrying no published usage figure of any kind.

context_window.note: The one thing that got BETTER. OpenAI's plan table now publishes a per-plan context window for every consumer tier — Instant 27K/54K/54K/128K and Reasoning Varies/256K/256K/400K across Free/Go/Plus/Pro. It is the first absolute product number any provider has ADDED rather than withdrawn in the period we have tracked. It bounds one conversation, not how many you get, so it does not close the allowance gap.

price_change.note: Consumers do better than developers here. The consumer Terms of Use commit that 'if we increase our subscription prices, we will give you at least 30 days' notice and any price increase will take effect on your next renewal so that you can cancel'. The business/developer Services Agreement is shorter and blunter: 'Price changes on the Pricing Page will be effective fourteen days after they are posted.'
price_change.source: OpenAI Terms of Use + Services Agreement (both read directly)

model_retirement.note: The strongest retirement commitment of any provider: a published deprecations page promising minimum notice of at least 6 months for generally available models and at least 3 months for specialized variants, with preview models explicitly carved out at around 2 weeks. Quantified, tiered, and stated as a floor.

rate_card.note: Per-token rates published on its own pricing docs and re-verified there on 2026-08-24. Also handled an intro-rate expiry honestly: Sonnet 5's $2/$10 launched as an introductory rate, and rather than letting it lapse quietly the pricing page states the scheduled 2026-09-01 rise to $3/$15 will not occur.

allowance.note: Across 27 consumer plans from 8 providers, 26 publish no usage allowance at all. Every paid tier is sold on a relative multiplier against a base nobody quantifies. Anthropic's four consumer plans all sit in that 26. Max is sold as '5x/20x more usage than Pro' with Pro itself unquantified, and the Consumer Terms say plan limits are 'described in the order process' while the terms themselves specify none.
allowance.source: claude.com/pricing; Anthropic Consumer Terms; Legerly plan-limits.json

context_window.note: No per-plan context window published for consumer tiers — the figure exists for the API but not for what a Pro or Max subscriber actually gets. OpenAI is currently alone in publishing this.

price_change.note: Quantified on both sides and read directly. Consumer Terms: fees will not change during a current term, and 'if these changes result in an increase in the fees payable by you, we will inform you at least 30 days in advance', with the increase applying at renewal so it can be cancelled first. Commercial Terms: updated rates take effect 'the earlier of 30 days after the updates are posted or Customer otherwise receives Notice'.
price_change.source: Anthropic Consumer Terms + Commercial Terms (both read directly)

model_retirement.note: A published lifecycle page committing to at least 60 days' notice before retirement for publicly released models — a shorter floor than OpenAI's, but paired with something no one else does: a forward 'not sooner than' retirement date for every ACTIVE model, most of them a year or more out, plus a complete deprecation history back to 2024. In practice that is more usable than the 60-day floor implies.

rate_card.note: Per-token rates published on its own Gemini API pricing page, re-verified 2026-08-24 — at which point 3.6 Flash and the new 3.7 Flash had been put on a half-price promotional rate with a stated end date of 2026-12-31. Dating the promo is the right behaviour; an undated promotional rate is a trap.

allowance.note: Across 27 consumer plans from 8 providers, 26 publish no usage allowance at all. Every paid tier is sold on a relative multiplier against a base nobody quantifies. Google's five consumer tiers are sold as '2x/4x/20x higher than standard limits', with its own footnote clarifying that the base is non-AI subscribers. It also reserves the right to change limits 'without notice, including due to capacity constraints'.

context_window.note: No per-plan consumer context window published.

price_change.note: Verified on Google's own Google One terms, which govern its AI subscriptions: “We will give you at least 30 days’ prior notice of a price increase before you are charged.” It also publishes the remedy if it misses that — “if you are given less than 30 days’ prior notice, the change will not apply until the payment after the next payment is due” — which is a stronger construction than most peers, because it says what happens when the commitment is broken rather than only stating the commitment.
price_change.source: Google One Additional Terms of Service (read directly)

model_retirement.note: A deprecations page exists, which puts Google ahead of five providers here, but it carries NO quantified commitment. Shutdown dates in the table are explicitly 'the earliest possible dates on which a model might be retired', with a promise only to 'communicate the exact shutdown date with advance notice' — advance notice of unspecified length. A date you cannot rely on and a notice period with no number.

rate_card.note: Per-token rates published on its own model docs and re-verified there 2026-08-24, including the higher above-200k-context tier.

allowance.note: Across 27 consumer plans from 8 providers, 26 publish no usage allowance at all. Every paid tier is sold on a relative multiplier against a base nobody quantifies. All five xAI consumer tiers are in that count.

context_window.note: No per-plan consumer context window published.

price_change.note: Verified on xAI's own consumer Terms of Service: “If prices increase, we will provide 30 days’ notice, and the new price will apply at your next renewal, allowing you to cancel if you disagree with the change.” Worth noting against the environmental axis above, where xAI is 🔴 on all six dimensions: the axes are genuinely independent, and a company can be opaque about water while being straightforward about billing.
price_change.source: xAI consumer Terms of Service (read directly)

model_retirement.note: Publishes retirement events properly but commits to no notice period. Its May 15 2026 retirement page names every retired slug, the redirect target, the exact cut-off time, and — usefully, and more than most disclose — the pricing impact: requests to a retired slug after the date are billed at the replacement model's rate. That is real operational disclosure. What is missing is a policy: nothing states how much warning the next retirement will carry, so you cannot plan, only react.
model_retirement.source: xAI model retirement migration guide (read directly)

rate_card.note: The clearest case on this table of a published price that is not the price. Perplexity publishes per-token Sonar rates — but they EXCLUDE a $5–14 per 1,000 requests fee which, for ordinary chat-shaped use, exceeds the token cost itself. A user pricing their usage off the published rate card would materially understate their bill. The number is disclosed; the cost is not.

allowance.note: Across 27 consumer plans from 8 providers, 26 publish no usage allowance at all. Every paid tier is sold on a relative multiplier against a base nobody quantifies. Perplexity's three consumer tiers are in that count.

context_window.note: No per-plan consumer context window published.

price_change.note: The only major provider whose price-change commitment carries no number. Its Terms of Service say only that “any price changes or changes to your subscription plan will take effect following reasonable notice to you.” Reasonable is not a period you can plan around, and it is unenforceable in any practical sense — the same unquantified-promise pattern that keeps Google's deprecation page at 🟡. Every other provider here except DeepSeek states a figure.

model_retirement.note: No notice-period policy, no forward retirement dates, and no lifecycle page — retirements surface as changelog entries, in at least one case recorded as already having happened (“Gemini 3.1-flash-lite-preview has been retired”). A log of what was removed is not notice of what will be. There is a structural reason worth stating fairly: Perplexity resells other providers' models, so some retirements are forced on it upstream and outside its control. That explains the position; it does not make the user any better informed.
model_retirement.source: Perplexity docs changelog (read directly); no lifecycle policy found

rate_card.note: Not applicable in the same form and therefore not graded: Copilot is sold as a subscription and Microsoft publishes no per-token consumer rate card of its own, reselling model access rather than pricing it directly. Grading this 🔴 would punish a different business model rather than measure disclosure.

allowance.note: Across 27 consumer plans from 8 providers, 26 publish no usage allowance at all. Every paid tier is sold on a relative multiplier against a base nobody quantifies. Both Microsoft consumer tiers are in that count.

context_window.note: No per-plan consumer context window published.

price_change.note: Verified in the Microsoft Services Agreement §9.j: at least 15 days' notice by email or other reasonable manner before a price change, applied at the next renewal, with a cancel-before-it-takes-effect right, and fixed-term locked-in prices exempt. Graded 🟢 because it is published, quantified and usable — but it is half the 30 days five other providers commit to, and that difference is stated here rather than hidden behind the badge. This axis grades disclosure, not generosity.

model_retirement.note: Consumer Copilot does not expose or version the model you are talking to, and Microsoft publishes no model-retirement notice policy for it. What it does announce, ad hoc through blog and message-centre posts, is FEATURE retirement — Deep Research and Podcasts both retired in consumer Copilot on 2026-08-18. Graded 🔴 rather than ⚪ (unlike the rate-card cell, where per-token pricing genuinely does not exist for this product) because the gap here is real and consumer-affecting: the model underneath can change without the user being told, or being able to tell.
model_retirement.source: Microsoft Copilot plans + retirement announcements; no model-lifecycle policy found

rate_card.note: Per-token rates published on its own pricing page and re-verified 2026-08-24. Also the only provider here publishing a student price ($5.99/mo) rather than routing students through an eligibility wall.

allowance.note: Across 27 consumer plans from 8 providers, 26 publish no usage allowance at all. Every paid tier is sold on a relative multiplier against a base nobody quantifies. Both Mistral consumer tiers are in that count.

context_window.note: No per-plan consumer context window published.

price_change.note: Verified on Mistral's own consumer terms, and it commits the same 30 days as the majors in both its rest-of-world and EU versions: “If we increase our prices, we will give you at least thirty (30) days’ notice and any price increase will take effect the next time your subscription renews … so that you can cancel if you do not agree.” The EU version adds that notice is sent by email to the account address.
price_change.source: Mistral ROW + EU consumer Terms of Service (both read directly)

model_retirement.note: The surprise of this axis. Mistral publishes a model lifecycle policy with a quantified notice period per stage — General Availability 6 months, Public Preview 1 month, Labs 1 month, third-party models 1 month — and states that the model stays accessible throughout the deprecation window. Its 6-month GA commitment equals OpenAI's and beats Anthropic's 60-day floor. It also maintains a dated deprecation table with retirement dates and named replacements. The smallest provider on this table has among the best disclosure on it.
model_retirement.source: Mistral model lifecycle policy + deprecation table (read directly)

rate_card.note: Per-token rates published on its own API docs and re-verified 2026-08-24, including its peak/off-peak split.

allowance.note: Across 27 consumer plans from 8 providers, 26 publish no usage allowance at all. Every paid tier is sold on a relative multiplier against a base nobody quantifies. DeepSeek's consumer tier is in that count.

context_window.note: No per-plan consumer context window published.

price_change.note: Warned, but barely. DeepSeek told developers on 2026-08-06 that a significant API price increase was coming, WITHOUT stating the new rate or the date; the increase landed on 2026-08-16, roughly ten days later, at 3–4.5× the previous rates. A warning with no number and no date is better than a silent change and materially worse than the 30 days OpenAI and Anthropic commit to. We had recorded the warning before it landed, and it landed as recorded.
price_change.source: DeepSeek API docs + pricing announcement; Legerly prices.json history

model_retirement.note: Announces retirements with a forward date and reasonable lead time, but has no published policy. Its updates page carried “the two legacy API model names, deepseek-chat and deepseek-reasoner, will be discontinued in three months (2026-07-24)” — three months of warning, dated, on its own docs. Better lead time than its price-change behaviour, where a rise landed roughly ten days after a warning that named neither rate nor date. Held at 🟡 because one well-handled instance is not a commitment.
model_retirement.source: DeepSeek API docs updates page (read directly)

site_level.note: Re-read 2026-08-25 against the 2026 Environmental Report (FY2025) — our previous note was a reporting cycle out of date and understated this. Google publishes withdrawal, discharge AND consumption for 36 named data center locations across eight countries (US, Ireland, Netherlands, Denmark, Finland, Belgium, Chile, Canada), plus an aggregated “other locations” bucket — up from 24 locations. It remains the most complete site-level disclosure of any provider, and it is stronger than Microsoft's on the two points that matter: Google publishes consumption, not just withdrawal, and the table sits inside the third-party limited-assurance scope rather than outside it.
site_level.source: Google 2026 Environmental Report, “Water use by data center location” (read directly)

ai_split.note: Re-checked 2026-08-25: the per-prompt figures are unchanged — median Gemini Apps text prompt at 0.24 Wh, 0.03 gCO₂e and 0.26 mL water, measured as of May 2025. The 2026 report adds that per-prompt energy and carbon fell 33× and 44× over twelve months, but facility reporting still does not split AI from general load, so the AI share of that 13,562 Mgal data-center withdrawal remains unknowable.

comparability.note: Still reports no fleet-wide WUE — now conspicuous, because both Microsoft (0.27 L/kWh) and Meta (0.19) publish one, so Google is the only major operator whose water efficiency cannot be compared with peers. Per-prompt figures still use market-based carbon and exclude indirect water; UC-Riverside's Shaolei Ren said Google is “just hiding the critical information.” Publishing per-location consumption answers part of that critique, not the indirect-water part.
comparability.source: Google 2026 Environmental Report (read directly); The Verge / DCD

replenishment.note: Replenished 78% of the freshwater it consumed in 2025 (9,947 Mgal consumed, 7,717 Mgal replenished), against a stated goal of 120% by 2030 — a real number, published, and trending up. Still graded 🟡 because replenishment is reported by watershed but returned water often sits in different watersheds than those drawn down, so the fleet figure does not mean local supply was made whole.
replenishment.source: Google 2026 Environmental Report, freshwater replenishment table (read directly)

energy_source.note: Achieved ~65% global average carbon-free energy in 2025 (up from 64%), and at least 80% CFE in 9 of 22 grid regions — reported by region, which is better than any peer. But it is still a market-based accounting method, and total emissions are now 62% above the 2019 base year, up from the ~51% we recorded last cycle. The trend line and the headline percentage point in opposite directions.

verification.note: 2025 metrics were subject to third-party limited-assurance procedures, and — unlike Microsoft — that scope covers the granular per-location water table, not just the headline aggregates. Held at 🟡 rather than 🟢 because limited assurance is the weakest form of it and covers selected metrics only; we are not going to call limited assurance “good” for anyone.
verification.source: Google 2026 (FY2025) Independent Accountants’ Review Report (scope legend read directly)

site_level.note: Re-read 2026-08-25; our previous note said “no site-level and no historical tables” and both halves were wrong. AWS publishes a public per-Region table giving PUE for 2022–2025 and WUE for 2024–2025 by named Region (e.g. US East N. Virginia 1.15 PUE / 0.06 WUE; Europe Ireland 1.10 / 0.02). That is company-published, dated and comparable — but it is efficiency ratios only, with no absolute water or energy volume per Region, and many Regions still show N/A for WUE. Absolute figures exist as a single global total (2.5B gal withdrawn, 2025) and, at Region/service/account granularity, only inside a paying customer's AWS Sustainability Console — visible to customers about their own workloads, not to the public. Graded 🟡: real named-location disclosure, but ratios for everyone and volumes only for customers.
site_level.source: AWS Region PUE and WUE table (read directly); AWS Sustainability Console blog

ai_split.note: Re-checked 2026-08-25 against the 2025 Amazon Sustainability Report: still no AI-vs-total breakout. The report discusses AI-driven cooling load at length — the In-Row Heat Exchanger, a projected 9% water reduction versus evaporative cooling — without ever attributing a volume or a kWh to AI.

comparability.note: Now publishes a consistent multi-year efficiency series — global WUE 0.25 → 0.19 → 0.18 → 0.15 → 0.12 L/kWh across 2021–2025, global PUE 1.14, plus the per-Region table — which is genuine year-on-year comparability and moves this off 🔴. The cherry-pick stands, though: the headline claim that 0.12 is “over 7× better” than an 0.84 industry average sets Amazon's whole fleet against other operators' power-intensive AI-specific facilities, and Amazon publishes no AI-specific figure of its own to compare like for like.
comparability.source: Amazon 2025 Sustainability Report + AWS Region table (read directly); DCD

replenishment.note: Reports 75% progress toward its water-positive-by-2030 goal (up from 53% and 41% in the two prior years), 45 replenishment projects, an expected 22B+ litres returned annually and $1B committed to public water infrastructure. Moved 🔴→🟡 for consistency: the offsets-in-other-communities critique that keeps Google and Microsoft at 🟡 applies here too, and it should not cost Amazon an extra grade. Worth remembering how it got here — a leaked internal plan showed intent to keep data-center water use secret, and the global total only appeared in 2026. What would earn 🟢 is watershed-level reporting that matches what was returned against what was drawn down.

energy_source.note: Publishes global PUE 1.14 (2025) and per-Region PUE back to 2022, names ISO 50001-certified Regions, and counts its portfolio (264 solar, 109 wind, two nuclear projects). Matched to Microsoft's 🟡 for the same reason and the same limitation: the renewable claims rest on market-based energy attribute credits, and the actual grid mix at any given AI facility is not disclosed. Efficiency is well covered here; energy *source* is not.
energy_source.source: Amazon 2025 Sustainability Report + AWS Region PUE table (read directly)

verification.note: Limited assurance over selected metrics, with a Data Tables and Assurance Statements section in the 2025 report, and a separately published assurance statement covering the water-withdrawal methodology behind the Sustainability Console. Same ceiling as every peer — selected metrics, limited assurance, not the whole inventory.
verification.source: Amazon 2025 Sustainability Report, Data Tables and Assurance Statements; AWS assurance statement

site_level.note: Confirmed 2026-08-24 by reading Microsoft's own 2026 Environmental Data Fact Sheet. Table 15, “FY25 Datacenter water and electricity use by location”, publishes electricity consumption (MWh), water withdrawal (ML), the non-potable share and replenishment volume for 29 named locations. That is the company disclosing it itself, so this row moves 🔴→🟢 — the first grade movement this index has recorded, and it makes Microsoft the second provider after Google to publish location-level figures. Four limits stop it short of Google's: the unit is a metropolitan area or regional cluster, not an individual building; the water metric is withdrawal, not consumption (consumption stays global/regional in Table 14); scope is Microsoft-owned datacenters under its own operational control, so leased and colocation capacity — including the QTS-built Fairwater Atlanta — is excluded; and Table 15 sits in Section 2, which the fact sheet states was outside Deloitte's limited-assurance review. Some values are Microsoft's own estimates where utility data was unavailable, by a disclosed methodology.
site_level.source: Microsoft 2026 Environmental Data Fact Sheet, Table 15 (read directly)

ai_split.note: Re-checked 2026-08-24 against both the full report and the fact sheet: still no AI-vs-total split. The new per-location table reports total datacenter electricity and water, not the AI share of either.
ai_split.source: Microsoft 2026 Environmental Data Fact Sheet (read directly)

comparability.note: Reports WUE consistently (0.27 L/kWh, 2025; down from 2.3 historically) and now publishes withdrawal per location, but still declares “water positive” while keeping consumption global and regional only (Table 14). Withdrawal is not consumption, so the new table does not close this gap.
comparability.source: Microsoft 2026 Environmental Data Fact Sheet; Trellis

replenishment.note: Still claims fleet-wide “water positive” via replenishment offsets, many in watersheds other than those drawn down. But the 2026 fact sheet now reports replenishment volume per named location and marks with an asterisk the priority locations that have delivered no volumetric benefit yet. Publishing the split — including where it is still zero — is what moves this off 🔴: the watershed mismatch is now checkable by anyone instead of buried in one global figure.
replenishment.source: Microsoft 2026 Environmental Data Fact Sheet, Table 15 (read directly)

energy_source.note: Now publishes electricity consumption (MWh) per named location, which is new and real. Still no per-site grid mix: renewable matching and hydrogen-backup pilots are described, but what actually powers the AI sites stays opaque.
energy_source.source: Microsoft 2026 Environmental Data Fact Sheet, Table 15 (read directly)

verification.note: Deloitte & Touche LLP performed a limited-assurance review of Section 1 of the fact sheet only. The per-location datacenter table is in Section 2, which the fact sheet states was not subject to that review — so the most granular figures Microsoft publishes are also its least assured. WUE methodology is published.
verification.source: Microsoft 2026 Environmental Data Fact Sheet, §1.11 + scope note (read directly)

site_level.note: Re-read 2026-08-25 against the 2025 Sustainability Report and its Environmental Data Index; our previous note was materially out of date. Meta does now report by site: per-facility electricity consumption (MWh) and per-facility market- and location-based GHG emissions for every named data center back to 2020, and the Index states owned, online data centers are always reported by site. Water is the gap — sections 3.1–3.4 give withdrawal, consumption and discharge by source, by intensity and by water-stress area, but there is no per-facility water table. Held at 🟡 because per-site water is the disclosure every 🟢 in this column was earned on. This is now a strong 🟡, not the near-🔴 it used to be.
site_level.source: Meta 2025 Environmental Data Index, §2.1 and §3.1–3.4 (read directly)

ai_split.note: Re-checked 2026-08-25 across both the 2025 Sustainability Report and the Environmental Data Index: no AI-vs-total split anywhere. Per-facility electricity gets you closer than most — you can see which campus draws what — but nothing attributes any of it to AI.
ai_split.source: Meta 2025 Sustainability Report + Environmental Data Index (read directly)

comparability.note: Reports both PUE (1.08) and annual data-center WUE (0.19 in 2024, down from 0.30 in 2020) on a consistent multi-year basis — more comparable efficiency reporting than Google, which publishes no fleet WUE. Held at 🟡 for two reasons: absolute water is still aggregate-only, and Meta's latest data is calendar 2024, a full year behind Google's FY2025, so a like-for-like comparison isn't actually available.
comparability.source: Meta 2025 Environmental Data Index, §2.4 and §3.1 (read directly)
